name: Media & Streaming
one_liner: Studios, networks, and streaming services that monetize content through subscriptions and advertising, with economics driven by content spend and subscriber retention.
how_it_makes_money: Streamers earn monthly subscription fees, increasingly supplemented by ad-supported tiers, while traditional networks earn carriage fees from cable distributors plus advertising. Studios also license content to third parties, sell theatrical tickets, and monetize franchises through merchandise and theme parks.
revenue_formula: Ad revenue = hours viewed × ad load × fill rate × CPM
Subscribers = prior subs + gross adds − churned subs
cost_structure: Content: original production and licensed rights, including costly sports rights, is the dominant cost
Marketing: subscriber acquisition and title launches
Technology and delivery: streaming platform, CDN, and product development
Talent and residual payments to creators and unions
margins: Scaled leaders can earn operating margins of roughly 20-30%, while subscale streamers have struggled to break even. Scale, content efficiency, churn, and ad monetization drive the spread.

key_metrics.name: Subscribers
key_metrics.what: Paid accounts; the headline measure of reach, though some companies now de-emphasize it.

key_metrics.name: ARPU
key_metrics.what: Average revenue per subscriber; reflects price increases, ad-tier mix, and geography.

key_metrics.name: Churn
key_metrics.what: Share of subscribers cancelling each month; high churn inflates acquisition costs.

key_metrics.name: Engagement (hours viewed)
key_metrics.what: Time spent watching; drives retention and ad inventory.

key_metrics.name: Content spend efficiency
key_metrics.what: Viewing or subscriber gains per dollar of content; tests programming decisions.

key_metrics.name: CPM
key_metrics.what: Price advertisers pay per thousand impressions; key to ad-tier economics.

trends: Streamers shifting from subscriber growth to profitability through price increases and password-sharing crackdowns
Ad-supported tiers becoming a core growth driver
Accelerating cord-cutting eroding linear TV carriage and ad revenue
Consolidation, bundling, and spin-offs of legacy cable network assets
Live sports moving to streaming platforms
Competition for attention from YouTube, short-form video, and creators; generative AI entering production

case_angles.question: A streaming service's subscriber growth has stalled; how can it return to profitable growth?
Should a streamer launch a cheaper ad-supported tier?
Should a media company bid for a major sports league's streaming rights?
Should two legacy media companies merge?

interview_hooks: Is streaming consolidation inevitable, and who survives as a standalone?
Does live sports justify its escalating rights costs?
Is YouTube the real winner of the streaming wars?
